articles.title: US World Leaders Perceive Donald Trump's Time in Office as Limited
articles.summary: Donald Trump's authority is being challenged from multiple fronts due to the recent electoral reversal in the United States.
articles.content: The shift in global politics may be taking shape as world leaders begin to see Donald Trump's time in office as limited, and this perception could have far-reaching implications for his ability to influence international relations. As a result of the recent electoral reversal in the United States, where the governing party suffered its most significant defeat in over half a century, Trump's authority is being challenged from multiple fronts. The president still retains significant executive power, but even that has its limits, and now the constraints on his ability to dominate the global agenda are becoming increasingly clear. The notion that Trump's presidency is entering a new phase was proposed by Ian Bremmer, founder of Eurasia Group and GZERO Media, who believes that America has reached "peak Trump. This does not mean the president is powerless, but rather that his influence is being curtailed by growing opposition from within Congress and among Republicans. Trump's unpopular economic and foreign policy decisions have also taken a toll on his ability to shape global events. Furthermore, world leaders are starting to see him as a short-term figure, with only two years left in office before the next presidential election. As Trump's power wanes, international relations may begin to shift towards more traditional alliances and partnerships, potentially altering the dynamics of global politics. The implications of this development could be far-reaching, but it is too early to say exactly how they will play out. The reversal in fortunes for President Trump has been nothing short of remarkable. He engineered a stunning comeback in 2024, but now finds himself facing what Bremmer describes as his biggest loss in 50 years. At the heart of this turnaround lies a crucial distinction between the formal powers of the presidency and the president's ability to wield them effectively. While Trump retains his position as commander-in-chief and continues to dominate the media landscape, his capacity to turn these advantages into lasting policy outcomes is rapidly diminishing. The consequences of this shift are being felt far beyond Washington's borders. The ongoing conflicts in Iran and Ukraine, as well as strained transatlantic relations, are prompting America's allies and adversaries alike to reassess their strategic calculations. They are beginning to look beyond the present administration towards the post-Trump era. Foreign leaders are now starting to engage more with the United States in a way that reflects the country they expect to deal with after Trump leaves office. As Trump's presidency enters its final stretch, his dwindling popularity and perceived lack of focus on key issues are taking a toll on his ability to shape global policy. The president's preoccupation with monuments, personal projects, and his own legacy has sparked concerns about the impact on governance. This spectacle of power is increasingly overshadowing the substance of decision-making, raising questions about the effectiveness of Trump's leadership. Economic disillusionment at home, coupled with allegations of corruption and self-dealing reminiscent of America's Gilded Age, are eroding the electoral coalition that put Trump in office. The president's inability to sustain the demands of the presidency is also becoming apparent, with many observing a decline in his focus on critical issues. The implications of this trend for American democracy and the international order are profound, as Trump continues to wield significant constitutional powers despite his waning influence. His ability to shape global policy will soon be severely tested, with foreign leaders already adapting their strategies to prepare for a post-Trump era. The presidency's two-year time frame is now a stark reminder of Trump's limited tenure in office. As Bremmer suggests, it appears that peak Trump" may have already reached its climax, marking a turning point in his ability to shape global policy. articles.title: Martine Rose appointed creative director of Balenciaga
articles.summary: London-based designer Martine Rose has been named creative director of Balenciaga, effective November 16.
articles.content: London-based designer Martine Rose has been appointed as the new creative director of Balenciaga, effective November 16. This highly anticipated move comes after years of speculation about her potential involvement with the French fashion house. Rose's relationship with Balenciaga began in 2015 when she worked as a menswear consultant for the brand, helping to shape its aesthetic under Demna's direction. Her tenure at the company was marked by the introduction of oversized silhouettes that have since become a hallmark of the label. She will succeed outgoing creative director Pierpaolo Piccioli, who departed on Thursday after just three seasons in the role. This marks a significant milestone for Rose, who is set to become the first female creative director at Balenciaga in its 109-year history. Rose's appointment has been welcomed by Kering CEO Luca de Meo, who praised her "fresh, fearless and deeply contemporary vision." He noted that she will bring a new dimension to the house with her connection to the younger generation and instinctive understanding of culture. Gianfranco Gianangeli, president and CEO of Balenciaga, has hailed Martine Rose as an extraordinary creative talent with a bold and highly distinctive vision. He praised her ability to challenge conventions and bring an unexpected perspective to fashion, qualities that align perfectly with the brand's innovative spirit. Rose's appointment has been met with widespread enthusiasm across the industry, with scores of editors, stylists, influencers, and celebrities taking to social media to express their excitement online. Her eponymous label, launched in 2007, has garnered a loyal following for its offbeat menswear inspired by British subcultures. Rose's influence extends beyond her own brand, as she has been name-dropped by high-profile fans including Kendrick Lamar, Rihanna, A$AP Rocky, and Timothée Chalamet. These celebrities have all been spotted wearing her oversized, sports-infused fits in recent years, underscoring the designer's ability to transcend fashion boundaries. The timing of Rose's appointment at Balenciaga is particularly opportune, given her existing momentum as a designer and creative force. With her unique vision and perspective, she is poised to make a significant impact on the brand's future direction. The appointment of Martine Rose as Creative Director of Balenciaga has been met with significant challenges in her own business ventures. At her eponymous label, Rose faced major difficulties after selling a 60% stake to incubator Tomorrow Ltd in 2023, leading to a public dispute over the handling of her brand. The tension between Rose and Tomorrow Ltd came to a head when she announced that she would not produce her FW26 collection, only for Tomorrow Ltd to release a counter statement and ultimately produce the collection despite Rose's decision. This was followed by another major development in March this year, when Tomorrow Ltd sold Rose's brand to Italian company The Level Group. Balenciaga's understanding of the current generation's tastes is unmatched among luxury brands, according to a statement made by the company during its Capital Markets Day in April. Martine Rose shares this insight, evident in her ability to create best-selling items that resonate with Gen Z, from affordable T-shirts to collaborations like her ongoing partnership with Nike. The luxury industry has been struggling to adapt to changing consumer preferences, and Balenciaga is looking to revitalize its appeal by embracing a more inclusive approach, as seen in Rose's high-low aesthetic. Rose's expertise in men's fashion makes her well-suited to take the helm of Balenciaga's menswear business, which was a key area of growth under Demna's leadership. Balenciaga's accessories division is expected to receive increased attention under Rose's leadership, particularly in leather goods, which have become the brand's top growth driver. The Rodeo and City bags are leading this charge, and de Meo aims to further accelerate the leather goods business by 2030. Rose expressed her gratitude for being appointed creative director of Balenciaga, acknowledging its rich heritage and fearless approach to creativity. This appointment is part of a broader reorganization at Kering, which includes the departures of Anthony Vaccarello from Saint Laurent and Seán McGirr from Alexander McQueen. The successors to these roles have yet to be announced, but speculation suggests that women may fill both positions, potentially making Kering a conglomerate with majority-women creative directors by year's end. articles.title: Asia's tech and AI landscape attracting significant investment
articles.summary: The region is seeing a surge in startup funding, with $42.8 billion invested in the second quarter of 2026 alone.
articles.content: Asia's tech and AI landscape is rapidly evolving, attracting budding entrepreneurs from around the world. According to Magnus Grimeland, founder and CEO of venture capital firm Antler, the continent has become a hub for startups due to its unique advantages. At the Fortune Southeast Asia 500 Summit in Vietnam on November 3rd, Grimeland emphasized that Asia offers real benefits for tech companies. Unlike previous platform shifts, where building from the US was often the preferred choice, Grimeland believes that this time there are genuine advantages in Asia. He pointed out that the continent is home to a vast pool of talent and resources. Data from Crunchbase reveals a significant surge in startup funding across Asia, with investors pouring $42.8 billion into the region in the second quarter of 2026 alone. This represents the highest quarterly total in over three years, underscoring Asia's growing importance as a hub for tech innovation. A rapidly expanding electricity grid and access to advanced chips and AI engineering talent are key factors driving Asia's appeal to startups, according to Grimeland. He noted that global power production has shifted towards Asia, with four times more power being generated and built in the region than in Europe and the US combined. The cost of power has also decreased dramatically in Asia compared to other regions, making it an attractive location for companies looking to expand or establish operations. This trend is particularly pronounced in China, where a significant portion of the continent's energy production takes place. The trend of building and developing artificial intelligence (AI) technologies is shifting towards Asia, where significant advancements are being made. One area where this shift is particularly pronounced is in physical AI, such as autonomous vehicles. A number of leading companies in the field of autonomous vehicles are based in Asia, with one company in China reportedly having more autonomous vehicles on its streets than the rest of the world combined. This contrasts sharply with the situation in the US, where there are very few autonomous vehicles currently in operation. Despite this growth in AI innovation, venture funding in Asia remains unevenly distributed. According to Dealroom data, a significant majority of VC funds entering Asia so far in 2026 have flowed into China, primarily into AI startups such as DeepSeek and Moonshot AI. The disparity in funding is also evident when comparing China to Southeast Asia, where only $10.7 billion of venture funding has been allocated during the first nine months of the year, a stark contrast to the $96.1 billion invested in China. The unique business landscape in Asia has created an environment where venture capitalists can invest in infrastructure development alongside innovative startups. In developing markets like the Philippines, investors often focus on building foundational systems that support entrepreneurship, rather than simply backing established innovators who have access to existing resources. This approach is reflected in the investment strategy of Foxmont, which has launched themed funds targeting specific areas such as digitization in the Philippines and accessibility for Filipino consumers. The region's venture firms are also adapting their models to meet the needs of Asian businesses, many of which are family-owned or part of conglomerates that prioritize strategic capital over equity dilution or public listings. Granite Asia's Libra Hybrid private credit fund is one example of this trend, offering a hybrid financial instrument that combines debt and equity characteristics to provide companies with flexible growth capital. The trend of building innovative companies from Asia is gaining momentum, particularly in the AI sector. Panelists at a recent discussion agreed that this shift presents a unique opportunity for entrepreneurs and investors alike. Asia's VC scene has shown resilience despite recent geopolitical challenges. As innovation continues to spread across the continent, it's likely that many groundbreaking companies will emerge from Asian soil.
